title: Three Ways to Persuade
objective: After this level you can identify appeals to character, emotion and reason: Aristotle's ethos, pathos and logos.
summary: Aristotle sorted persuasion into three kinds: the speaker's character (ethos), the hearer's emotions (pathos) and the argument itself (logos). Only logos is an argument you can check.

cards.headline: Three ways to sell you an umbrella on a cloudy day
cards.body: The shopkeeper can remind you she has sold umbrellas for years. She can make you picture your good shoes soaked through. Or she can show you the forecast. Three different kinds of pull, and Aristotle sorted persuasion into exactly these three. His list still works.

cards.headline: Character, feeling, argument
cards.body: In his Rhetoric, Aristotle said persuasion comes through three means: the character of the speaker (ethos), the emotional state of the hearer (pathos), or the argument itself (logos). The shopkeeper's years behind the counter are ethos. Your soggy shoes are pathos. The forecast is logos. One pitch can use all three, so the useful skill is telling them apart.

mascot.line: Keep this: ethos is the speaker, pathos is the listener, logos is the argument. Three places to look.

cards.headline: Ethos: why should I trust you?
cards.body: Persuasion by character works when the speech makes the speaker seem worth believing. Aristotle named three things that inspire that confidence: good sense, good moral character and goodwill toward the audience. His twist: it has to be done by what the speaker says, not by what people thought of them beforehand. Credibility is earned in the speech itself.

cards.headline: Pathos: the mood changes the verdict
cards.body: Aristotle noticed that our judgments when we're pleased and friendly are not the same as when we're pained and hostile. A judge who feels friendly toward the accused thinks they did little wrong; a hostile judge thinks the opposite. That's why speakers stir feelings: feelings shift judgment. Same facts, different mood, different verdict.

cards.headline: Logos: the argument itself
cards.body: The third means persuades through proof, or apparent proof, in the words of the speech. It's the only one of the three built like Level 5's arguments, with premises and a conclusion. Notice the word "apparent": logos can be a bad argument dressed up well. Checking which it is, is logic's job.

cards.headline: Three appeals: sorted
learned: Ethos persuades through the speaker's character
Pathos persuades through the hearer's feelings
Logos persuades through the argument itself
Only logos has premises and a conclusion

questions.prompt: Which of Aristotle's three means of persuasion works through the speaker's character?

options.label: Pathos
options.rationale: Pathos works through the hearer's emotions.

options.label: Kairos
options.rationale: Kairos isn't one of the three means on the card.

questions.explanation: Ethos is persuasion through the character of the speaker.

questions.prompt: How does pathos persuade, on Aristotle's account?

options.label: By stirring feelings that shift the hearer's judgment
By showing the speaker has good sense
By deriving a conclusion from premises
By repeating the claim until it sticks
options.rationale: Repetition isn't one of Aristotle's three means.

questions.explanation: Emotions change judgment: a friendly judge and a hostile judge see the same case differently.

questions.prompt: Which of Aristotle's three appeals is built like a Level 5 argument, with premises and a conclusion?

options.label: Ethos
options.rationale: Ethos works through the speaker's character, not premises.

options.label: Pathos
options.rationale: Pathos works through the hearer's feelings.

options.label: All three equally
options.rationale: Only one of the three has an argument's structure.

questions.explanation: Logos persuades by proof or apparent proof: premises offered for a conclusion.
